title: Painful, deformed hands in a 41-year-old man on the rheumatology ward
desc: This station involves a focused history and a musculoskeletal hand examination of Jack Peralta, a 41-year-old café owner. He was admitted overnight to the rheumatology ward with a flare of painful, swollen hands, and his old notes cannot be found. In Part 2 the candidate interprets his observations, his admission bloods and the only hand X-ray report on the system (from 2018). They then diagnose a flare of established seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis after he stopped methotrexate, plan bridging treatment and the restart of a DMARD, and counsel him on methotrexate safety.
focus: Systematic hand examination: recognising the deformities and synovitis of rheumatoid arthritis, telling it from other hand arthropathies, reading a rheumatoid hand X-ray and planning DMARD treatment safely
stem: You are a medical student on the rheumatology ward of a metropolitan hospital. Jack Peralta, a 41-year-old man, was admitted overnight with painful hands. The consultant asks you to assess his hands and report your findings. The team cannot find his old notes. His clinic records from before 2019 were on paper and cannot be located; only an old imaging report is on the electronic system.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Peralta and perform a focused examination of his hands, telling the examiner what you are examining and describing your findings as you go (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you his observations, his blood results and a hand X-ray report. Interpret them. Give a handover including your interpretation, state your diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Jack Peralta, a 41-year-old man who runs a café with your partner. Your full name is Jack Peralta and your date of birth is 14 March 1985 (you are wearing a hospital wristband with these details). You are sitting up in bed holding your hands carefully in your lap. You are tired and sore, but friendly and keen to get home. You are right-handed. Give the history below only when asked. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "My hands have been really bad for the last few weeks. I can barely do my buttons up."

The current problem (give only when asked)

  • Joints: both hands (the knuckles and middle finger joints) and both wrists, the same on both sides. The balls of both feet are sore too. The end finger joints are fine.
  • Onset and course: it started about 3 weeks ago and has got steadily worse. The joints look puffy and feel warm.
  • Character and severity: "A deep, throbbing ache." 6 out of 10 now, 8 at its worst first thing in the morning.
  • Morning stiffness: "About two hours before I can really use my hands." It eases as the day goes on and with gentle use.
  • Function: you cannot grip a coffee jug, open jars, do up buttons or write properly. You have not been able to work at the café for 2 weeks.
  • Why you came in: the pain was keeping you awake and you could not manage at home, so you went to ED last night and were admitted.
  • Fatigue: "I'm wiped out all the time."

Things you do NOT have (say no if asked)

  • No fever, sweats or shakes. No single joint much worse than the others. No cuts or wounds on your hands.
  • No numbness or pins and needles in your fingers. No weakness. No weight loss.
  • No cough, breathlessness or chest pain.
  • No red or painful eyes. If asked about dry eyes: "They feel a bit gritty sometimes."
  • Neck: "A bit stiff in the mornings." No pins and needles or weakness in the arms or legs, and no trouble with your bladder or bowels.
  • No psoriasis, scaly rash or nail changes. No diarrhoea or blood in the stool. No facial rash, mouth ulcers or hair loss. Your fingers do not go white or blue in the cold.
  • You have never had a sudden, very painful red joint or gout.

Past medical history

  • "I've got rheumatoid arthritis." It was diagnosed when you were 29, at this hospital. You were seen in the rheumatology clinic here until 2019, when you moved to the country. Your GP there kept prescribing your tablets.
  • "I had a few courses of prednisone tablets years ago when it flared." Only if asked: "They talked about injections once, but then I moved." You have never had a biological medicine.
  • You moved back to the city 8 months ago to open the café. You have not found a new GP or rheumatologist yet.
  • No liver or kidney problems, no stomach ulcers, no lung problems, no operations.

Medications and allergies

  • You used to take methotrexate 20 mg once a week (on Mondays) and folic acid. You stopped about 5 months ago. "My old GP retired, I ran out, and to be honest it made me feel sick the day after, so I didn't rush to get more."
  • For the last 3 weeks: ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day and paracetamol 1 g up to four times a day, both bought at the chemist.
  • No known drug allergies.
  • Vaccinations (only if asked): a flu shot at the chemist last year. "No idea about the others." You do not know whether you have been tested for hepatitis.

Family history

  • Your mother has an underactive thyroid. No one in the family has rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis or gout that you know of.

Social history

  • You smoke 15 cigarettes a day and have since you were 18.
  • Alcohol: 4 to 6 beers on a Friday and Saturday night, none during the week.
  • You run a café with your partner, Sam. You live with Sam and your 6-year-old son. Sam is covering the café but it is a struggle.
  • No recreational drugs.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Ideas: "I know it's my rheumatoid playing up because I stopped the tablets."
  • Concerns: losing the café if you cannot work, and your fingers getting more bent. "Are my hands going to end up useless?"
  • Expectations: you want the swelling down quickly so you can go home and get back to work. You are wary of going back on methotrexate because of the nausea.

During the examination

  • If the candidate squeezes your knuckles or bends your wrists without warning, wince and pull back a little. If they ask about pain first and are gentle, you cooperate fully.
  • If asked something not covered here, give a realistic answer that fits the story.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they are examining)

Examiner: read these as descriptions. Do not supply the names of the deformities; the candidate must name them.

  • Vital signs (08:00 nursing set): temperature 36.9 °C, HR 88 beats/min regular, BP 128/78 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air. Weight 84 kg.
  • General inspection: looks tired, normal build. No Cushingoid features, no bruising or thin skin. No splints or walking aids in use (he has old wrist splints at home).
  • Eyes and face: mild conjunctival pallor. No scleritis, episcleritis or iritis. No malar rash, alopecia or mouth ulcers.
  • Elbows and forearms: no nodules, no rash, no psoriatic plaques.
  • Arms above the head: he can do this with mild discomfort in both shoulders, full range.
  • Hands, inspection (dorsal): in both hands the fingers angle towards the little finger at the knuckles, and the bases of the fingers sit lower than the knuckles. Right index and middle fingers and left middle finger: the middle joint is bent backwards and the end joint is bent down. Both thumbs: bent at the base knuckle and bent backwards at the end joint. Visible swelling of both wrists, the 2nd and 3rd knuckles of both hands and several middle finger joints. Firm lumps over the backs of several middle finger joints and knuckles. Hollowing between the long bones on the back of both hands. No scars, rash, bruising or nail-fold infarcts. No swelling or bony enlargement of the DIP joints; no Heberden's nodes. Nails normal: no pitting, ridging, onycholysis or hyperkeratosis. No tophi. Skin not tight or shiny; no dactylitis.
  • Hands, inspection (palms): mild redness of the palms over the base of the thumb and little finger. No thenar wasting. No palmar crease pallor. No Raynaud's changes or digital ulcers.
  • Palpation: both wrists, the 2nd and 3rd MCP joints of both hands, the right 2nd and 3rd PIP joints and the left 3rd PIP joint are tender, with soft, warm, spongy swelling. Squeezing across the knuckles is painful in both hands. The lumps over the joints are firm, rubbery, mobile and non-tender. DIP joints are normal. Make a fist: incomplete, with the fingertips 2 cm short of the palm in both hands.
  • Movement: wrist flexion and extension reduced to about 40° each way, painful at the end of range, with crepitus. The angling of the fingers at the knuckles and the bent finger and thumb deformities do not straighten when you try to correct them passively.
  • Special tests: Tinel's and Phalen's tests are negative on both sides. Sensation is normal in the median, ulnar and radial distributions.
  • Thumb movements and strength: thumb flexion, extension, abduction and opposition are present but weak. Grip strength, opposition (pinch) and key grip are all weak on both sides.
  • Function: he struggles to do up a button, writes slowly and untidily, and cannot open a jar.
  • Feet: the MTP squeeze is tender on both sides, with swelling across the forefoot. No callosities or ulcers.
  • Other joints: elbows, shoulders, knees and ankles have no effusion or synovitis. Neck (if examined): mildly reduced rotation, not tender; arm and leg power, sensation and reflexes normal.
  • Cardiovascular and respiratory: dual heart sounds, no murmur, no pericardial rub. Chest clear, no fine crackles. No lymphadenopathy, spleen not palpable.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self as a medical student, confirms his identity with two identifiers (his notes are missing) and gains consent for the history and examination.
Asks about pain before touching. Positions both hands on a pillow, exposes the arms to the elbows, asks him to remove rings and watch, and examines gently.
Acknowledges his pain and his worry about the café and his hands, uses plain language, and describes the findings to the examiner as they go.
History
Characterises the current flare:

kids.x: Joints: both hands (MCPs, PIPs) and both wrists, plus the balls of both feet; symmetrical; end finger joints spared.
Onset and course: 3 weeks, steadily worse, with puffy, warm joints.
Asks how long morning stiffness lasts: about 2 hours.
Function: cannot grip, do buttons, write or work at his café; right-handed.

check.x: Establishes the past history the notes cannot give: rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed at 29 at this hospital, followed in this rheumatology clinic until 2019, then managed by a GP in the country.

Takes the treatment history: methotrexate 20 mg once weekly with folic acid, stopped about 5 months ago (ran out when his GP retired, and nausea the day after each dose). Past prednisone courses, never a biological medicine.
Current medicines and allergies: over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day and paracetamol for 3 weeks; no known drug allergies.
Screens for infection: fever, sweats, one joint much worse than the others, and cuts or skin breaks on the hands (none).

Screens for extra-articular features and complications: dry or red, painful eyes, cough or breathlessness, chest pain, numbness or tingling in the fingers, neck pain with tingling or weakness in the limbs, fatigue and weight loss.
check.d: Credit if 3 or more areas are asked.

check.x: Screens for other causes of a deforming hand arthritis: psoriasis or nail changes, bowel symptoms, rash, mouth ulcers, hair loss or Raynaud's phenomenon (SLE), and previous attacks of gout.
check.d: Credit if 3 or more are covered by question or by stated examination negatives (nails, plaques, facial rash, alopecia, ulcers, tophi).

check.x: Asks about the factors that affect restarting methotrexate: alcohol intake, liver or kidney disease, hepatitis B or C status or risk, and vaccinations.
check.d: Credit if 2 or more are asked. Hepatitis status or vaccination may also be credited if the candidate raises it in the Part 2 management answer.

check.x: Social and family history: smokes 15 a day since 18 (about 17 pack-years), 4 to 6 beers on Friday and Saturday nights, runs a café, lives with his partner and 6-year-old son. No known family history of inflammatory arthritis or psoriasis.
check.d: Credit if smoking, alcohol and occupation are covered.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations. He thinks the flare is from stopping his tablets, fears losing the café and his hands getting worse, wants the swelling down quickly, and is wary of methotrexate nausea.
Examination
Requests vital signs (afebrile, normal) and does a general inspection: normal habitus, tired, no Cushingoid features, no bruising, no splints or aids.
Inspects the eyes and face: mild conjunctival pallor; no scleritis or iritis, facial rash, alopecia or mouth ulcers.
Screens the elbows and forearms (no nodules or psoriatic plaques) and asks him to raise his arms above his head (shoulders move fully).
Inspects the backs and palms of both hands and describes:

kids.x: Ulnar deviation of the fingers with subluxation at the MCP joints of both hands.
Swan neck deformity (right index and middle, left middle finger) and Z-deformity of both thumbs.
Firm, rubbery nodules over several PIP and MCP joints.
Swelling of the wrists, MCPs and PIPs, dorsal interosseous wasting and palmar erythema. States the DIPs are spared, with no Heberden's nodes, nail pitting or onycholysis, tophi or tight skin.
kids.d: Credit if DIP sparing and at least two of the negatives are stated.

check.x: Palpates the wrists, MCPs, PIPs and DIPs. Identifies warm, boggy synovitis of both wrists, the 2nd and 3rd MCPs and several PIPs, a painful MCP squeeze, normal DIPs and an incomplete fist.
Assesses movement: wrist range reduced and painful, with crepitus. States the finger deformities cannot be fully corrected passively (fixed).
Performs Tinel's and Phalen's tests (negative) and checks sensation and thumb movements. Tests grip, opposition and key grip (all weak).
Assesses hand function with at least one practical task (buttons, writing or a jar).
Examines the feet (tender MTP squeeze) and states they would complete the assessment with the other joints, cervical spine, heart and lungs.
check.d: Credit the heart and lungs if stated rather than performed.

check.x: Interpretation
Observations: all in the white zone, afebrile, with no clinical review or rapid response criteria, which fits a polyarticular flare rather than systemic infection. His pain still needs addressing.
Interprets the bloods:

kids.x: CRP 46 and ESR 58: active inflammation, fitting a flare.
RF 128 and anti-CCP 250, both strongly positive: seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, a marker of more severe, erosive disease.

Hb 118 with a normal MCV and platelets 452: likely anaemia of chronic disease with reactive thrombocytosis; requests iron studies given his NSAID use. Normal LFT and kidney function mean methotrexate can be restarted.

check.x: Checks the X-ray details: name and date of birth, and confirms they match Mr Peralta's identifiers; and the date (7 November 2018, nearly 8 years old). States that current X-rays of the hands and feet are needed to show his disease now.

Reads the X-ray: ulnar deviation of the digits with radial deviation at the carpus, subluxation of all MCP joints, loss of joint space, and erosions at the MCPs and PIPs. Concludes established erosive rheumatoid arthritis.
States the diagnosis: an active flare of established seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis, with fixed deformities and rheumatoid nodules, after stopping methotrexate 5 months ago.
Gives at least 3 differentials, each with a reason for or against: psoriatic arthritis, chronic tophaceous gout, SLE with Jaccoud's arthropathy, septic arthritis.
check.d: Credit 3 or more, each with a reason.

check.x: Management

Controls the flare now: analgesia, and a short bridging course of corticosteroid (oral prednisolone tapered, or an intra-articular injection into the worst joints), as agreed with the rheumatology team.

Restarts methotrexate once weekly on a named day, building back to his previous dose, with folic acid on a different day, and offers a strategy for his nausea (e.g. subcutaneous methotrexate, evening dosing, an antiemetic, or more folic acid).
check.d: Weekly dosing and a nausea strategy are required for the mark.

check.x: Orders the pre-treatment checks: hepatitis B and C serology (and HIV if at risk) and a baseline chest X-ray. Reviews his vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, zoster).
check.d: Credit if hepatitis B serology and at least one other check are named.

check.x: Plans treat-to-target care, aiming for remission or low disease activity, escalating via the rheumatologist (combination csDMARD, then a PBS-subsidised bDMARD or tsDMARD) if still active.
Involves an occupational or hand therapist and a physiotherapist, and addresses smoking (Quitline, nicotine replacement).
Explains in plain words that the bent fingers are permanent damage that medicine will not straighten, but that regular treatment can switch off the inflammation and prevent further damage.
Safety netting

Gives specific red flags: same-day review for fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers, bruising or bleeding, new cough or breathlessness, jaundice; ED for a single hot swollen joint with fever or neck pain with limb tingling or weakness.
check.d: Credit if 3 or more are named in plain words.

check.x: Explains methotrexate safety: once a week only, never daily; no trimethoprim or co-trimoxazole (Bactrim); tell every doctor and pharmacist he takes it; limit alcohol to no more than 1 to 2 standard drinks, once or twice a week, and avoid binge drinking: his 4 to 6 beers on Friday and Saturday nights is binge drinking and needs to come down to that limit.
check.d: Weekly dosing must be stated for the mark.

check.x: Arranges follow-up: rheumatology clinic in 4 to 6 weeks and regular blood monitoring with a new GP (FBC, LFT and UEC every 2 to 4 weeks for the first 3 months or after a dose increase, then every 1 to 3 months).
check.d: Credit clinic review and regular bloods with a new GP; the exact interval is not required for the mark.

part2.lead: Here are Mr Peralta's observations from this morning, his admission blood results, and the only hand X-ray report the team could find on the imaging system.
part2.patient:
During the fourth question, as the candidate explains, Mr Peralta asks each of these once:

  • "Will my fingers ever straighten out again?"
  • "That methotrexate made me feel sick the day after. Do I really have to go back on it?"

If the candidate uses jargon ("DMARD", "synovitis", "erosions"), ask "What does that mean?" once. He agrees to restart methotrexate once the candidate explains why it matters and offers a way around the nausea.

handover.label: Observations (ward)
handover.result: Room air throughout. 08:00 and 10:00 routine nursing sets on the morning after admission.
handover.model:
Read: at 08:00, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, BP 128/78, HR 88 regular, temperature 36.9 °C, alert, pain 6/10. At 10:00 the readings are similar (BP 124/76, HR 84, temperature 37.1 °C, pain 6/10). Every value is in the white zone of the adult chart at both times, so there are no clinical review or rapid response criteria.

For Mr Peralta: he is afebrile and haemodynamically normal. With synovitis in many joints on both sides, this fits an inflammatory flare rather than septic arthritis or systemic infection.

What it changes: no escalation is needed and observations continue routinely. Pain of 6/10 still needs regular analgesia and treatment of the flare. A new fever, or one joint becoming much hotter than the others, would need review for infection, especially once immunosuppression restarts.

rows.note: Morning set; hands and wrists painful and stiff

handover.label: Admission blood results
handover.model:
Read: CRP 46 and ESR 58 are raised. RF 128 IU/mL and anti-CCP 250 U/mL are both strongly positive. Hb 118 with a normal MCV of 86, and platelets 452, raised. White cells and neutrophils are normal. Sodium, potassium, urea and creatinine are normal, with eGFR above 90. Liver function is normal and albumin 36 is at the lower end of normal.

For Mr Peralta:

  • The raised inflammatory markers show active disease, which fits a flare.
  • Strong seropositivity, especially anti-CCP, confirms rheumatoid arthritis and predicts erosive, more severe disease. It also argues against psoriatic arthritis, SLE and gout.
  • The normocytic anaemia and reactive thrombocytosis are likely anaemia of chronic disease. He has taken ibuprofen three times a day for 3 weeks and is about to start prednisolone, so request iron studies given his NSAID use (GI blood loss or mixed iron deficiency).
  • A normal white cell count does not exclude infection, but with normal observations infection is unlikely.

What it changes: normal liver and kidney function mean methotrexate can be restarted. These results are its monitoring baseline. Hepatitis B and C serology have not been done and are needed before restarting.

labs.title: Urea, electrolytes, creatinine and liver function

handover.label: X-ray of both hands (from the imaging system)
handover.result:
Patient: Jack Peralta. DOB 14/03/1985.

Examination: X-ray of both hands and wrists, PA views. Date of examination: 07/11/2018.

Clinical details: rheumatoid arthritis, review of progression.

Comparison: none available.

Findings:

  • Alignment: ulnar deviation of the digits at the MCP joints in both hands, with radial deviation at the carpus. Subluxation of all MCP joints.
  • Joint spaces: loss of joint space at the MCP and PIP joints and the wrists. The DIP joints are preserved.
  • Bone margins: marginal erosions at the MCP and PIP joints. No osteophytes.
  • Soft tissues: no soft tissue swelling. No soft tissue calcification and no chondrocalcinosis.
  • Other: no fracture.

Conclusion: erosive arthropathy of both hands, with ulnar deviation at the MCP joints, radial deviation at the carpus and MCP subluxation, in keeping with established rheumatoid arthritis.
handover.model:
Details: name and DOB match Mr Peralta's wristband, PA views of both hands and wrists, dated 7 November 2018. That is nearly 8 years old, with no comparison.

Read: bilateral ulnar deviation of the digits with radial deviation at the carpus (the zig-zag pattern). Subluxation of all MCP joints. Loss of joint space and marginal erosions at the MCPs and PIPs, with the DIPs preserved. No osteophytes, chondrocalcinosis or soft tissue calcification. No soft tissue swelling on that date.

For Mr Peralta: this is erosive rheumatoid arthritis that was already established in 2018. The deformities are structural and match his fixed deformities today. There are no features of osteoarthritis (osteophytes, DIP disease), gout (punched-out erosions with overhanging edges, tophi) or CPPD (chondrocalcinosis).

What it changes: the film cannot show today's disease. Request current X-rays of both hands and feet as a new baseline to judge progression. Erosive disease is a poor prognostic sign and supports intensive treat-to-target DMARD therapy.

ask: The consultant has come back to the ward. Please give an ISBAR handover of Mr Peralta, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Mr Peralta now, here on the rheumatology ward.
Mr Peralta will go home in a few days on methotrexate. What would you tell him before he goes, and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student on the rheumatology ward. Jack Peralta, 41, café owner.
  • Situation: admitted overnight with a 3-week flare of symmetrical hand, wrist and forefoot synovitis and 2 hours of morning stiffness.
  • Background: RA diagnosed at 29 here. Methotrexate 20 mg weekly stopped 5 months ago (ran out, nausea). Never on biologics. OTC ibuprofen. Smokes 15 a day. No drug allergies.
  • Assessment: symmetrical synovitis of wrists, MCPs, PIPs and MTPs; fixed RA deformities and nodules; DIPs spared. Obs white zone, afebrile. CRP 46, ESR 58: active disease. RF and anti-CCP strongly positive. Hb 118 normocytic, platelets 452: likely anaemia of chronic disease; iron studies given 3 weeks of ibuprofen. LFT and UEC normal. Hand X-ray (Jack Peralta, DOB 14/03/1985, matches wristband; PA both hands, dated 7/11/2018, nearly 8 years old): ulnar deviation at the MCPs with radial deviation at the carpus, MCP subluxation, joint space loss and marginal erosions at the MCPs and PIPs, DIPs preserved: established erosive RA. Old film, so it does not show current activity.
  • Recommendation: bridging steroid; restart weekly methotrexate after hepatitis serology; current X-rays of both hands and feet.

Most likely: flare of established seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis after stopping methotrexate. For it: symmetrical MCP, PIP, wrist and MTP synovitis; 2 hours of morning stiffness; fixed ulnar deviation, swan neck and Z-thumbs; rheumatoid nodules; DIPs spared; raised CRP and ESR; strongly positive RF and anti-CCP; marginal erosions on X-ray.

  • Psoriatic arthritis: erosive and can deform the hand, but no psoriasis or nail changes, DIPs spared, seropositive.
  • Chronic tophaceous gout: nodules over joints in a man, but rubbery not chalky, no acute attacks, no punched-out erosions, anti-CCP positive.
  • SLE with Jaccoud's arthropathy: swan neck and ulnar deviation, but fixed, erosive deformities and no rash, ulcers or Raynaud's.
  • Septic arthritis (must not miss): afebrile, symmetrical, no single joint out of proportion.

1. Symptoms: regular paracetamol. NSAID short term if no contraindication; add a PPI while on an NSAID with prednisolone. Resting splints.
  2. Bridge the flare: e.g. prednisolone 10–15 mg orally daily, tapered over several weeks (or IM/intra-articular methylprednisolone), per eTG and the rheumatology team.
  3. Before restarting: hepatitis B and C serology (HIV if at risk), baseline chest X-ray; review vaccinations.
  4. Restart methotrexate once weekly on a named day, e.g. 10–15 mg weekly, increasing by 2.5–5 mg every 2–4 weeks to 20 mg as tolerated. Folic acid on a different day, e.g. folic acid 5 mg once weekly, not on the methotrexate day (can be increased if he has nausea). Nausea strategy: subcutaneous route, evening dosing, an antiemetic or more folic acid.
  5. Treat to target: remission or low disease activity; escalate via the rheumatologist (combination csDMARD, then PBS bDMARD/tsDMARD) if still active.
  6. Team: OT or hand therapist, physio. Quit smoking (Quitline, NRT).

• Plain words: the bent fingers are old damage and will not straighten with medicine. Methotrexate switches off the inflammation and protects the joints; it takes a couple of months to work. Nausea can be reduced with injections, evening dosing, an anti-nausea tablet or more folic acid.
  • Safety: methotrexate once a week only, never daily. Folic acid on another day. No trimethoprim or Bactrim. Tell every doctor and pharmacist. Alcohol no more than 1–2 standard drinks once or twice a week, no binges; his 4 to 6 beers on Friday and Saturday nights is binge drinking and needs to come down to that limit.
  • Red flags, same-day review: fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, bruising or bleeding, new cough or breathlessness, yellow skin. ED: one hot, swollen joint with fever; neck pain with tingling or weakness.
  • Follow-up: rheumatology clinic in 4 to 6 weeks. FBC, LFT and UEC with a new GP every 2–4 weeks for 3 months or after a dose increase, then every 1–3 months.

ddx.dx: Flare of established seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis after stopping methotrexate
ddx.for: Symmetrical synovitis of the wrists, MCPs, PIPs and MTPs with 2 hours of morning stiffness, fixed ulnar deviation, swan neck and Z-thumbs, rheumatoid nodules, raised CRP and ESR, strongly positive RF and anti-CCP, and marginal erosions on X-ray.
An erosive, deforming polyarthritis of the hands in a 41-year-old man.
ddx.against: No psoriasis, nail pitting or onycholysis, no dactylitis, DIPs spared, and strongly positive RF and anti-CCP.

ddx.for: Nodules over the finger joints with an erosive arthropathy in a middle-aged man who drinks at weekends.
ddx.against: The nodules are rubbery rather than chalky, he has never had an acute attack, the erosions are marginal without overhanging edges, and anti-CCP is strongly positive.

ddx.dx: Systemic lupus erythematosus with Jaccoud's arthropathy
ddx.for: Swan neck deformities and ulnar deviation of the fingers.
ddx.against: The deformities are fixed and erosive rather than reversible, and he has no rash, mouth ulcers, hair loss or Raynaud's.

ddx.dx: Septic arthritis superimposed on rheumatoid arthritis
ddx.for: Rheumatoid arthritis is a risk factor, and he has warm, swollen joints with raised inflammatory markers.
ddx.against: Afebrile with normal observations, symmetrical involvement of many joints, and no single joint out of proportion or skin break.

guide:
The station takes place at about 10:15 on the morning after admission. In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. Read the hand findings as descriptions and do not name the deformities: items 20, 21 and 22 are earned only when the candidate supplies the labels (ulnar deviation, swan neck, Z-thumb, synovitis, fixed deformity). Allow about 4 to 5 minutes of history, then 5 to 6 minutes of examination. Prompt at 5 minutes if the candidate has not started examining. Credit findings only when the candidate describes them, and give the vital signs from the 08:00 set when asked.

In Part 2 read the lead, hand over all three results together, then ask the four questions in order. Mr Peralta puts his two questions during the fourth question. Credit item 29 if the candidate confirms the name and DOB match, notes the 2018 date and requests current hand and foot X-rays. Item 13 may be credited from the Part 2 management answer if hepatitis status or vaccination is raised there. Item 36 may be credited from the ISBAR or the management answer. Items 41 and 42 may be credited if they come up in the management answer.

A high-performing candidate establishes the RA history and the stopped methotrexate quickly, asks about morning stiffness, infection and extra-articular features, and then examines systematically. They prepare first (pain, pillow, exposure, jewellery) and do a general, face and elbow screen. They describe ulnar deviation, MCP subluxation, swan neck, Z-thumbs, nodules and DIP sparing, palpate for synovitis, test whether the deformities are correctable, and assess nerves, strength and function. In Part 2 they check the film's details and date, read the X-ray systematically and diagnose a flare of seropositive erosive RA. They plan bridging steroid, safe re-initiation of weekly methotrexate after hepatitis screening with a plan for his nausea, treat-to-target care and hand therapy, and give clear methotrexate safety advice.

A borderline candidate examines without screening the face, elbows or function. They call the nodules Heberden's nodes or tophi, do not separate synovitis from bony swelling, or miss the date on the X-ray. They may give steroids alone without restarting a DMARD, prescribe methotrexate without stating it is weekly, or give vague safety netting.
explain:
Diagnosis: flare of established seropositive, erosive rheumatoid arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, symmetrical, inflammatory polyarthritis of the synovium. It typically affects the MCP and PIP joints, the wrists and the MTP joints and spares the DIP joints. Inflammatory joint pain is worse after rest, with morning stiffness lasting more than 30 to 60 minutes, and eases with use. Fatigue is common. Untreated synovitis erodes cartilage and bone and stretches the joint capsule, ligaments and tendons, producing the fixed deformities Mr Peralta shows. His flare follows 5 months off methotrexate. Smoking is a risk factor for developing seropositive RA and is linked with more severe disease and a poorer response to treatment.

The hand examination

  • Prepare: ask about pain, rest the hands on a pillow, expose to the elbows, remove jewellery.
  • General and face: habitus, Cushingoid features from steroids, splints and aids. Pallor (anaemia of chronic disease), scleritis or episcleritis, dry eyes. Malar rash, alopecia and mouth ulcers (SLE).
  • Elbows and shoulders: rheumatoid nodules, psoriatic plaques; arms above the head for shoulder involvement.
  • Look: ulnar deviation and volar subluxation at the MCPs. Swan neck (PIP hyperextension, DIP flexion). Boutonnière (PIP flexion, DIP hyperextension, from rupture of the central slip). Z-thumb (MCP flexion, IP hyperextension). Also look for nodules, dorsal interosseous wasting, scars (previous tendon or joint surgery), bruising (steroids), vasculitic nail-fold infarcts and palmar erythema.
  • Patterns to tell apart:
    • Osteoarthritis: Heberden's (DIP) and Bouchard's (PIP) nodes and a squared thumb base.
    • Gout: tophi.
    • Psoriatic arthritis: plaques, nail pitting, ridging, onycholysis and hyperkeratosis, DIP disease, dactylitis.
    • Scleroderma: tight skin and sclerodactyly.
    • SLE: reversible deformities and Raynaud's.
    • Whether the DIPs are involved is the key discriminator.
  • Feel and move: make a fist. Palpate the wrists, MCPs, PIPs and DIPs for warm, boggy synovitis (soft) as opposed to bony swelling (hard), and do an MCP squeeze. Assess range and crepitus, and whether deformities correct passively.
  • Special tests and function: Tinel's and Phalen's tests (carpal tunnel syndrome is common in RA), thumb movements, grip, opposition and key grip, and practical tasks: buttons, writing, opening a jar.
  • Systemic: feet (MTP squeeze), other joints, heart (pericarditis) and lungs (interstitial lung disease, effusions), and the cervical spine. Atlantoaxial instability matters before anaesthesia or neck manipulation.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: all in the white zone and afebrile, so no escalation is needed. This fits a polyarticular flare, not sepsis.
  • Bloods: raised CRP and ESR show active disease. RF and especially anti-CCP are strongly positive. Anti-CCP is highly specific for RA and, like a high RF, predicts erosive disease. The normocytic anaemia and thrombocytosis most likely reflect chronic inflammation, but he has taken ibuprofen three times a day for 3 weeks and is about to start prednisolone, so request iron studies to look for GI blood loss or mixed iron deficiency. Normal liver and kidney function are the baseline for methotrexate.
  • X-ray: always check the name, date of birth, date and views first, and confirm they match the patient. This film is from 2018, so it shows past damage, not today's activity. Rheumatoid features are:
    • soft tissue swelling and periarticular osteopenia early
    • uniform loss of joint space
    • marginal erosions at the MCPs, PIPs and wrists
    • later, subluxation and the zig-zag deformity (ulnar deviation at the MCPs, radial deviation at the carpus).
    Compare osteoarthritis (LOSS: loss of joint space, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts) and gout (punched-out erosions with overhanging edges). New hand and foot X-rays give a current baseline.

Management (eTG Rheumatology: rheumatoid arthritis)

  • Symptom control: paracetamol, and an NSAID short term if there is no contraindication. Add a PPI while he is on an NSAID with prednisolone, as the combination raises GI risk. Resting splints.
  • Bridging corticosteroid: a short, tapering course controls the flare while DMARDs take effect, e.g. prednisolone 10–15 mg orally daily, tapered over several weeks (or IM or intra-articular methylprednisolone into the worst joints), per eTG and the rheumatology team. Avoid long-term use.
  • Methotrexate is the first-line DMARD.
    • Give it once weekly on one named day, with folic acid on a different day to reduce side effects, e.g. folic acid 5 mg once weekly, not on the methotrexate day (can be increased if he has nausea).
    • After a 5-month gap with nausea, restart at a lower dose and build up, e.g. 10–15 mg once weekly, increasing by 2.5–5 mg every 2–4 weeks to his previous 20 mg as tolerated.
    • Nausea can be managed by switching to subcutaneous methotrexate, taking it in the evening, an antiemetic, or a higher or more frequent folic acid dose (ARA patient information).
    • It takes weeks to months to work fully.
    • Before starting, check FBC, LFT and UEC, and do hepatitis B and C serology (HIV if at risk) and a baseline chest X-ray.
    • Monitor FBC, LFT and UEC every 2–4 weeks for the first 3 months or after a dose increase, then every 1–3 months (ARA).
  • Treat to target: measure disease activity (e.g. DAS28) and aim for remission or low disease activity. If methotrexate alone is not enough, combine conventional DMARDs (e.g. with sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine). If the disease stays active, a rheumatologist can prescribe a PBS-subsidised biological or targeted synthetic DMARD once the PBS criteria are met.
  • Vaccination before immunosuppression (Australian Immunisation Handbook): influenza, pneumococcal and COVID-19. Discuss zoster vaccine. Check hepatitis B status.
  • Team and long-term care: an occupational or hand therapist for splints, joint protection and aids, and a physiotherapist. Hand surgery may help selected function-limiting deformities. RA raises cardiovascular risk, and smoking worsens RA and reduces the response to treatment, so stop smoking (Quitline, nicotine replacement) and manage blood pressure and lipids.

Safety netting and follow-up

  • Weekly dosing: daily instead of weekly methotrexate dosing has caused deaths. State the weekly dose and day on every script and in every explanation.
  • Interactions and alcohol: avoid trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole, which increase the risk of bone marrow suppression. Limit alcohol to no more than 1–2 standard drinks, once or twice a week, and avoid binge drinking (ARA advice); his 4 to 6 beers on Friday and Saturday nights is binge drinking and needs to come down to that limit.
  • Same-day review for fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, bruising or bleeding (cytopenia), a new cough or breathlessness (pneumonitis), and jaundice.
  • ED for a single hot, swollen joint with fever (septic arthritis), or neck pain with limb tingling or weakness.
  • Follow-up: rheumatology clinic within 4 to 6 weeks; FBC, LFT and UEC with a new GP every 2–4 weeks for the first 3 months or after a dose increase, then every 1–3 months; a discharge letter; and current X-rays of the hands and feet as a new baseline.
points: Examine the hands in order: prepare (pain, pillow, exposure, jewellery), general and face, elbows and shoulders, then look, feel and move, special tests and function, and finish with the feet, heart, lungs and cervical spine.

Rheumatoid arthritis gives symmetrical boggy synovitis of the wrists, MCPs and PIPs with DIP sparing, morning stiffness over 30 to 60 minutes, and with time ulnar deviation, MCP subluxation, swan neck, boutonnière and Z-thumb deformities. Fixed deformities and erosions separate it from the reversible Jaccoud's deformities of SLE.

DIP involvement points away from RA, towards osteoarthritis (Heberden's nodes) or psoriatic arthritis (nail pitting, onycholysis). Firm rubbery nodules suggest rheumatoid nodules; chalky deposits suggest tophi.

On a rheumatoid hand X-ray, check the details and date first. Then look for soft tissue swelling, periarticular osteopenia, uniform joint space loss, marginal erosions and subluxation with the zig-zag deformity. An old film does not show current disease activity.

Strongly positive anti-CCP and RF confirm RA and predict erosive disease. Treat a flare with a short bridging corticosteroid, but disease control comes from DMARDs: methotrexate first line, treated to target, escalating to combination or biological therapy.

Methotrexate is taken once weekly, never daily, with folic acid on another day. Screen for hepatitis B and C before starting, monitor FBC, LFT and UEC, avoid trimethoprim, and tell patients to seek review for fever, mouth ulcers, bruising or a new cough.
